brief: The town stops progressing. maturity() pins at day 8 and richness() at day 16, so at DAY_LEN 55 s every growth term is at 1 by real minute 15 and there is no later act — the weather and the market days keep turning over, but a viewer who leaves this open for forty minutes sees the same town they saw at fifteen. Give the world ONE slow cyclic scalar, season(), on the same footing as cloudCover() and isWindy(): a 0..1 phase over a multi-day cycle, with the cycle length chosen so a full turn is legible in roughly 20-30 real minutes, and rate-capped so no sample ever steps. Then give it at least two readers in the sky in this same iteration. The first is the length of the day itself: daylight is currently a fixed sin over hour in updateClock, so let the season move that window and a winter day is genuinely short. The second is the light — skyCols, sunVec, the dawn and dusk palette — a low cold sun against a high warm one. Because daylight feeds capacity, laneCap, eastCap and all three spawn rates, the town's population will breathe with the year for free. That is the whole reason to do it here, and it is also the risk.
successLooksLike: A filmstrip sampled one frame per sim-day across a full cycle shows the light turning and coming back with no step between frames, and __census().clock carries season so any probe can pin a point in the year. Two wide shots half a cycle apart are obviously two different times of year.
avoid: Do NOT simply raise the day-8 and day-16 caps in maturity()/richness(). That stretches the same one-way ramp and the town still stops, just later — the season must be cyclic. Do not make it a boolean or a four-way enum; this town's idiom is ramps, and the rate-cap law is what makes continuity provable by probe. Do not add a census field per reader — one `season` on the clock is enough. And set a floor: the shortest day must still leave the town populated and legible, because someone arriving in deep winter must not find a dead diorama. Measure population across a full cycle and state the trough.
